messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya Chandrasekaran was thirty-two years old and had spent the better part of her adult life in public service, first as a community organizer in a mid-sized Midwestern city and then, after a hard-fought election campaign, as one of its youngest city council members. Her work required her to be present — at town halls, ribbon cuttings, late-night budget sessions, public hearings in buildings she had never visited before. She had always understood that visibility was the price of the job, and she had paid it willingly. That changed on the evening of a municipal infrastructure summit fourteen months ago, when a gas explosion tore through the civic center where she and roughly three hundred other attendees had gathered. The blast originated in a utility corridor adjacent to the main hall. The lights failed immediately. In the darkness and smoke, the crowd surged toward exits that were partially blocked by debris, and Priya was pressed against a wall for what felt like several minutes, unable to move, unable to see, listening to the sounds of people screaming and the groan of the building settling around her. She escaped with lacerations and a fractured wrist. Eleven people did not escape at all.

In the weeks that followed, Priya told herself she was managing. She returned to council sessions within a month, though she found herself arriving early to every meeting so she could walk the room before it filled — locating the exits, noting which doors opened outward, positioning herself on the aisle closest to the rear of the chamber. What had begun as a precaution hardened into compulsion. By the time she sought help, she could not enter any space — a restaurant, a community center, a colleague's office — without first conducting a systematic survey of its exits and identifying the fastest path out. She avoided unfamiliar venues entirely when she could, and when her schedule required her to attend events in buildings she did not know, the anticipatory dread could begin days in advance. Her chief of staff had quietly begun routing her away from off-site meetings, telling other officials that the councilwoman had scheduling conflicts. She had not told him why.

The explosion had left Priya with a settled and unshakeable conviction that the world was a dangerous place and that safety, wherever it appeared, was provisional. She had come to believe that vigilance was not a symptom but a rational response to reality — that the only people who felt safe were people who had not yet been hurt. This belief was the engine driving nearly everything that had organized itself around her fear. Because she was certain she had to be on guard at all times, she scanned every room she entered for people whose behavior seemed off, tracked movement at the edges of crowds, and sat with her back to walls when she could manage it. She avoided any situation that might tax her physically — not because she feared injury in isolation, but because she understood, with a logic that felt airtight, that a body already under stress could not respond fast enough if something happened.

The behaviors she had built to manage her sense of threat were, in practice, sustaining it. Each time Priya checked the exits, mapped the room, or positioned herself near a door, she left the situation having confirmed only that danger was real enough to prepare for. The scanning never produced reassurance; it produced more scanning. Nights were worse than days — something about darkness returned her, without warning, to the civic center corridor — and she had largely stopped accepting evening engagements, which in a city council role was professionally untenable. Her sleep was poor, her concentration fractured, and a colleague had recently asked, with visible concern, whether she was all right.

It was that question, more than anything, that brought her to the intake appointment. She was not afraid of being seen as weak, she said carefully — she was afraid that if she let her guard down long enough to accept help, something would happen that she had not prepared for. What she hoped for, she admitted after a pause, was to stop living as though the explosion were still occurring. She was not sure she believed that was possible.
